items.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for sauteed cabbage with cheese cream and sunflower seeds
items.summary:
A rich, comforting plateful of sweet, crunchy hispi topped with a cheesy cream – like a bowl of pasta, only without the carbs

This is a fun recipe that takes advantage of the hispi cabbage’s sweet nature and pliant structure. You can give it a really hard blast of heat, and it will crisp, caramelise and smoke, but still retain a lot of its easy freshness and bright crunch; it will also take on a pleasing, slightly slippery texture, like buttered noodles. This plate has the satisfaction of a hearty bowl of pasta without being nearly so enervating, and it works fantastically as a side dish, too, either as a companion to toasted whole grains or some grilled mushrooms.

Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London

items.summary:
Cold pears stained red with tart hibiscus and offset by a hot, creamy, spiced rice pudding

Hibiscus has a tart, berry-like flavour, and turns these pears a jewel-bright crimson in colour. The pears are best poached a day ahead, because they’ll deepen in colour and flavour while they chill in the syrup. I especially like the contrast of the cold, gently tangy pears against a warm, creamy rice pudding that’s fragrant with cardamom, bay, lemon and vanilla. A scattering of pistachios adds a final touch of both colour and crunch.

items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for torta tenerina, or rich chocolate cake | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary:
This soft-but-dense, velvety delight is cake at its most pudding-like. It’s at its prime still warm from the oven, but gets gloriously fudgy after a night in the fridge

The note by Elizabeth David is helpful here: “This cake can also be eaten like a pudding” for its soft-dense-velvet-texture. But I am jumping ahead: this week’s column started in Ferrara, a city in the wetlands of the Po delta in the north-eastern corner of Emilia-Romagna. Half medieval lanes and half green avenues and parks, Ferrara is home to one of Europe’s most imposing red-brick castles, one that provides a home to an annual journalism festival run by the magazine Internazionale. Ferrara is also known for a cake. In fact, it was after a discussion about translation and fact-checking with the Italian writer Domenico Starnone and the translator Ann Goldstein that I first ate a wedge of chocolate, butter, egg, sugar and flour torta tenerina.

Having just mentioned fact-checking, I am now going to side-step the origin stories. The name, however, more or less translates as “little tender one”, although that “little” refers more to the fact that it is a bit tender, rather than being on the small side. Especially because tenerina recipes from Ferrara call for tins ranging from 24-26cm in size, which produce…

Rukmini Iyer, author of the bestselling cookbook series Roasting Tin, answered your queries from ideas for simple weeknight meals that can be prepped in 15 minutes to leftovers for lunches and whether one pan is always better than two

Ask a question: log in or sign up here

Swinehead asks: Is it better not to use baking paper (even though it is easier to clean up afterwards) so as to get a better “roasting” of ingredients? I find when I’m baking paper, the ingredients tend to be more “steamed” on true fan cooking.

Rukmini: Hello! Interestingly, my pal the food stylist Lu Cottle introduced me to the baking paper in a frying pan technique, where you fry things on a layer of oiled baking paper to prevent sticking in eg not a non-stick pan. You get tremendously brown, crisp results (for fritters etc) so I think it is possible for things not to steam, but this might be because of the direct heat of the pan.

In the oven, if you’ve found baking paper makes things steamier, then I’d not use it. But also to avoid steaming, use as shallow a tray as you can – the high sides plus lining paper might be the issue. items.title: Chicken curry and potato croquettes: Ranie Saidi’s recipes for a Malaysian feast
items.summary:
Leeks play a major part in two Malaysian-inspired dishes: they melt into coconut in a marvellous chicken curry, and pair perfectly with peas in crunchy potato croquettes

Since moving from Malaysia to London more than a decade ago, I’ve slowly brought leeks into my everyday cooking. Their gentle sweetness reminds me of banana shallots, and I love how they melt into this chicken gulai. Bergedil (or begedil or perkedel) have always been one of my favourite street-food snacks, and are found at stalls across Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. In Malay cooking, they’re often made using mashed potato that’s mixed with minced meat, shaped and fried, but my version uses leeks, frozen peas and leftover herbs, plus an orange, chilli and yoghurt dip.

items.summary:
Rye Bunny in Washington, D.C. | Rey Lopez/Eater 

These are the 15 new restaurants that best captured the year in dining. Our team of editors and scouts traveled across the country, drawing on years of experience to build the 2026 winners list. 

What we found remarkable: the quiet confidence of a chef who’s mastered Hungarian food in Pittsburgh; a fresh revamp of family-style Italian dining in Philadelphia grounded in the original restaurant’s 1950s roots; a cozy tribute to Southern cuisine in Denver that still manages to feel cool. What they have in common: a sincere commitment to making diners feel at home. — Missy Frederick , editorial director 

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here . 

Akoya Omakase 

Kansas City, Missouri 

“You went to Kansas City for sushi ?” I was asked more than once — with some derision — after returning from Missouri, so I can only imagine the uphill battle chef Peter Hoang faces at Akoya Omakase . Hoang isn’t easily daunted. He’s so committed to sourcing, he often personally drives to the airport to pick up the fish hand-selected by his two private buyers in Tokyo 26 hours after placing his order.

At Akoya, the fish quality is unassailable; the rice seasoned with precision. But Hoang consistently finds ways to complement Akoya’s sashimi and nigiri with unexpected accents. Smoky juvenile king mackerel gets a hit of acid and sweetness from pineapple chutney. Truffle, notorious for being overwhelming on just about anything, manifests in pate form alongside dashi and kelp salt to…

items.title: The 2026 Best New Bakeries in America
items.summary:
Parachute Bakery in San Francisco. | Ellen Mary Cronin/Eater 

If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game. 

Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick , editorial director 

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here . 

Bad Butter 

Chicago, Illinois 

If one new place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter . You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he launched his own online bakery business , earning a massive following along the way. 

One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. The Dougla Kitchen experience is epitomized by a crab-laden callaloo dip paired with crisp taro chips. | Nick Oxford/Eater 

Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category. 

From a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating. — Missy Frederick , editorial director

Puffed grain toast at All Well 

Chicago, Illinois 

When experiencing a five-course tasting menu ($145), I wasn’t expecting toast to be a main attraction. But even with competition from luxurious courses featuring everything from a complex Hokkaido scallop to an assertive charred rib-eye with peaches, All Well ’s puffed grain toast left a lasting impression. 

After three years at two-Michelin-starred Oriole , Larry Feldmeier partnered with Noah Sandoval, fellow Oriole alum and James Beard winner for Best Chef: Great Lakes , to open the ambitious West Loop restaurant All Well, which offers both a la carte bar options and the aforementioned tasting; the toast is only available as part of the latter experience.

items.title: The 2026 Chefs of the Year
items.summary:
An aguachile dish in progress at Maria Isabel. | Michelle Min/Eater 

Each of the chefs featured in our new national Chef of the Year category made news in a major way. But their most recent projects are just one part of their story. 

This year we celebrate five chefs who are making an impact both on the city where they cook and on the larger culinary conversation. — Missy Frederick , editorial director 

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here . 

Laura Ozyilmaz, Maria Isabel 

San Francisco, California 

San Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking. 

In the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel , the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history. 

Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican…

items.title: The Restaurants Already on Eater Editors’ Radar for 2027

A dish from the just-opened Alfie’s in D.C. | Alex McCoy 

Editors’ scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards , presented by Capital One, wrapped up at the end of August — just as fall restaurant-opening season was heating up. That means several notable restaurants that debuted in 2026 didn’t quite make the cut, either because they didn’t open in time or had only been open a matter of weeks and were still finding their footing as of our deadline. items.title: How to brighten up a school lunchbox | Kitchen aide
items.summary:
A bento box stacked with familiar and fun shapes, colours and textures beats a drab cheese and ham sandwich any and every day

I’m already struggling with lunchbox inspiration for the kids. Help!
Rachel, by email
This sounds like a job for Claudine Boulstridge, who has been packing lunchboxes for her three children for 15 years, which is to say she has her gameplan down pat: “Having a simple formula and a few go-to ingredients means I don’t have to reinvent the wheel every morning,” says the author of Family and the Healthy Family Food Substack. Well, that plus a bento-style box: “It keeps everything neatly separated, fresh and visually appealing for hours, without the hassle of small containers,” she adds. “So, even when I’m short on time, I can quickly fill the compartments with a variety of wholesome ingredients: crisp vegetables, juicy fruit, a chunk of cheese, a handful of nuts, a few slices of ham or salami … Lunch is sorted.”

More specifically, Boulstridge sticks to a formula of fruit (halved kiwi, orange slices, pomegranate, say), plus veg (cucumber, carrot, cooked sweet potato, radish), plus protein (soft-boiled egg, cheese, cooked chicken slices or drumsticks, hummus, fish cakes), plus a homemade snack (roast coconut flakes with cinnamon; seeds toasted with unsalted butter and spices; dried seaweed squares). And, just like getting dressed in the morning, accessories are the…

You can’t beat a creamy, tomato-based curry when you’re in need of comfort food, although chilli aficionados might want to up the amount of crushed red chillies from one teaspoon to two – or more.
